reference_opening.argument: The video and description jointly promote Pionex trading bots, direct viewers to a Pionex referral link, and present the speaker's own bot setup as a way to place money into an arbitrage strategy for a conditional one-percent weekly portfolio increase. This is an observed financial participation flow in which the speaker describes allocating funds to the bot and displays the corresponding 1,170-dollar setup, rather than merely discussing cryptocurrency or requesting ordinary audience engagement. The speaker does acknowledge that cryptocurrency carries substantial risk and that losses can occur, but the supplied records do not establish whether the stated return occurred, whether the service delivered it, or whether any viewer experienced a loss.

citations.quote: In this video i proceed with my journey where i will use a variant of FREE trading bots that are offered but the crypto exchange Pionex.
I just want to put in my money and let it run.
if my calculations are all correct I will increase my complete portfolio
one percent in one week so it's about 10 12 bucks
1170 dollars invested in this bot.

opening.argument: Judge, the strongest evidence against deceptive solicitation is the specific failure condition the speaker supplies: negative funding means closing the bot, and leaving it running can produce a loss. That is actionable risk disclosure, not merely a generic disclaimer. The projected portfolio increase is expressly contingent on his calculations being correct. He also exposes the initial negative result and identifies the opening fee rather than presenting an uninterrupted stream of gains. Read together, these statements support a demonstration of a fallible trading tool. A conditional estimate should not be treated as a guaranteed payout when the same demonstration explains both costs and a reason to stop trading.

citations.quote: If it's negative, close the bot. Just close it.
But there's a risk that it can happen. And then the bot will run in loss.
if my calculations are all correct I will increase my complete portfolio
At the moment we have 70 cents in loss. That's because we had to start, it's the opening fee.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The prosecution establishes capital allocation, but allocation alone does not establish deception. Its conditional-return quotation must be read alongside the explicit warning that the bot can lose money and should be closed when funding turns negative. The speaker is not simply attaching a vague caution to an otherwise unconditional promise; he identifies a concrete adverse operating condition. The prosecution also acknowledges that delivery and viewer losses remain unestablished. That evidentiary gap cannot turn a disclosed trading risk into proof of a scam.

citations.quote: Check if the funding fee is still positive. If it's negative, close the bot.
But there's a risk that it can happen. And then the bot will run in loss.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: Those warnings establish acknowledged risk, not the absence of promotion. The same speaker calls the approach really safe, describes a one-percent weekly return, and commits capital to the bot. The opening-fee disclosure does not verify that future earnings will materialize or neutralize the invitation to regard this funded bot as a return-producing strategy. A guarantee is not necessary to recognize the promotional mechanism: money is placed into the bot with an expectation of recurring profit.

citations.quote: It's a really safe approach after all.
one percent in one week so it's about 10 12 bucks
1170 dollars invested in this bot.

opening.argument: Judge, this is best understood as an operational demonstration with a planned follow-up, not proof of a completed investment opportunity. The description presents a personal series sharing what the creator learned. During setup, he reports the opening loss and its fee, then says he will return after seven days to inspect the profit. The sampled interface likewise shows a bot-details screen with investment and position information. These are features of a walkthrough: configuration, immediate costs, and a future evaluation. The proposed return is something to examine, not an independently established outcome. Classify the observed content by that instructional structure rather than treating the presence of funded trading software as sufficient evidence of a scam.

citations.quote: I will post updates on this series and will share what i learned that week.
At the moment we have 70 cents in loss. That's because we had to start, it's the opening fee.
I will be back when that counter is at seven days. And then we're going to see what profit we have.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The prosecution's own evidence is first-person: putting in my money, increasing my portfolio, and reporting an investment. Those statements establish the creator's demonstration, not an instruction that viewers must transfer funds. The omitted context is the promised later evaluation: he will return after seven days and see what profit exists. That makes the outcome an open question within the demonstration. A referral can coexist with a walkthrough; neither the referral nor a personal allocation resolves whether the content is deceptive.

citations.quote: I just want to put in my money and let it run.
I will be back when that counter is at seven days. And then we're going to see what profit we have.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: A walkthrough can also promote financial participation. Here, the description supplies an exchange signup referral, while the demonstration actually funds a bot and couples that allocation with a weekly return estimate. A promised follow-up does not make the current promotional mechanism disappear. The defense's fee and interface evidence shows how the investment is operated; it does not show that the presentation is merely neutral instruction or that the proposed return is substantiated.

citations.quote: Pionex Exchange with 12 FREE trading bots: https://www.pionex.com/en-US/sign/ref/nSrwtWes
1170 dollars invested in this bot.
one percent in one week so it's about 10 12 bucks

opening.argument: Judge, distinguish promotion of an exchange service from evidence of a fraudulent transaction. The description offers a Pionex signup referral and advertises free trading bots; the demonstrated allocation is described as the speaker's own money. The supplied bot-details frame shows a trading interface, not evidence that money is being diverted to the creator. His forecast is explicitly conditional on his calculations. These materials establish service promotion and personal use, but those cited elements do not establish a guaranteed payout, a recruitment-based income arrangement, or a demand to surrender credentials. That does not certify the exchange as safe. It means that a referral, a funded tool, and an uncertain estimate are insufficient by themselves to distinguish ordinary financial-service promotion from a scam.

citations.quote: Pionex Exchange with 12 FREE trading bots: https://www.pionex.com/en-US/sign/ref/nSrwtWes
I just want to put in my money and let it run.
if my calculations are all correct I will increase my complete portfolio

rebuttal.rebuttal: The prosecution identifies a financial participation flow, but that is also compatible with ordinary exchange-service use. The stated investment proves an allocation, not misappropriation; the referral establishes promotion, not a fraudulent payout mechanism. Its own return evidence is conditional. The disputed inference is therefore not whether a trading bot is funded, but whether these facts establish a scam. Without evidence resolving that distinction, service promotion should not automatically be treated as fraud.

Pionex Exchange with 12 FREE trading bots: https://www.pionex.com/en-US/sign/ref/nSrwtWes
if my calculations are all correct I will increase my complete portfolio

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The relevant mechanism is not credential theft or recruitment income. It is promotion of a funded trading bot through an exchange referral, a weekly earnings estimate, and demonstrated capital commitment. The defense's citations establish precisely those connected elements. Calling this ordinary service promotion overlooks how the speaker frames the investment as safe and expects money to be withdrawable from it. We need not invent diversion, completed payouts, or viewer losses to identify the observed return-oriented promotion.
